comments.text:
THIS HAPPENED TO ME!!!

I guessed fairly quickly only because I had such a similar experience when I was 7 yrs old. My only symptom for weeks was unexplained high fevers, which at some points caused audible hallucinations. I was eventually admitted into the hospital after the fever persisted and my WBC came back low. For days the mystery continued and I was poked and prodded multiple times a day with more tests than I could ever remember. Eventually they discoved some kind of tick born infection (not lymes but unsure of specifics as this was nearly 20 years ago). 

I would love to know your thoughts on long term effects with infections like this especially when the infection occurred as a child. I’m now 26 years old and was diagnosed with Fibromyalgia 4 years ago after experiencing symptoms since I was 16 or so. I have a laundry list of issues all said to be umbrelled under my fibromyalgia diagnosis, including hypoglycemia, temperature intolerance, fatigue, hyper mobility in my joints, lymphatic drainage issues, migraines, brain fog and some type of aphasia, and the list could go on. However these symptoms are made more manageable with a specific diet, OMT, monthly lymphatic drainage massages, duloxetine, and phentermine. 

I would really love to learn more about out this
comments.author: @reganpeterson1357

comments.text: Thank you for not giving up on your patient! I had a GI doctor years ago who, when all my blood work came back normal, he asked what else he could do for me. 🙄 What do you think you can do for me?! I feel terrible, help me feel better! He started pulling tests out of a hat that had nothing to do with my symptoms, and I could tell he was grasping at straws. I got the feeling he thought everything was normal from a testing standpoint, so why should I continue coming to him? I decided to switch doctors, and that doctor ordered some further testing (that applied to my symptoms). I ended up with a diagnosis of gastroparesis, which I'd never even heard of before. Thank goodness the 2nd doctor was willing to look for the zebras. I got on a strict diet, was put on some meds, and my symptoms got exponentially better. I really appreciate doctors who can think outside the box, and who don't dismiss people because their initial tests are all within normal range.

comments.text:
Hi Dr. Mike, I'm one of those zebras.

Got a gastric bypass in 2017, had a "idiopatic" pancreatitis in 2019, no alcohol intake and no gallstones have been found on ultrasounds. 

Been suffering from mouth ulcers and genital ulcers too.

It was a long road of ER (which is typical in Portugal, you go to ER almost everytime there's something wrong instead of a family doc) to discover a behçet disease, only got diagnosed last year, and we're still not done.

Ferritin, B12, folic acid, vit D are plummeted, so it's time to get infusions done.

We're still running differentials on this since I have a low grade fever every couple days and my autoimmune doctor wants to rule out haploinsufficiency A20 and possibly a limphoma.

All in all, what I have to say is thanks for sticking with your patients and not just dismissing their symptoms!

comments.text: I just dealt with a fever of unknown origin for 4 months. Blood work completely normal. Outside of fever and chills, felt fine. Doc thought it was my mastocytosis, but fever and chills aren’t my normal. Went to dermatologist to get something else checked out, found out the rash I thought was from my mastocytosis was actually a fungal infection. Used anti fungal cream for 2 weeks, symptoms completely resolved. No idea why my bloodwork was normal. I knew something wasn’t right, though. My dermatologist is great, everyone needs to have one! She also recently (earlier this year) found 2 suspicious moles during a routine exam, biopsied them right then and there, came back as pre cancerous melanoma. We were confused because I have a sun allergy so don’t even go outside during the day if I can help it, and most of my windows in my house are covered with either foil or cardboard so I don’t burn. Turns out systemic mastocytosis can cause skin cancer. Would have been nice to know sooner!

God, imagine being blessed enough to have a doctor who cares enough to look into things like this.

Here's what I've been told about accessing the ER:

My children get sick occasionally.  We have a phone line where they almost always advise going to the hospital. I no longer go.

comments.text: 9:19 I would disagree. EBV reactivation is almost always a bystander phenomenon triggered by another process rather than the primary cause of fever, so a concurrent process should have been considered either way. What should have heavily oriented towards anaplasmosis was the combination of leukopenia with a left shift and relative lymphopenia + thrombocytopenia + transaminitis (quite specific in a febrile patient for anaplasmosis). EBV mono would have typically caused leukocytosis with atypical lymphocytes, and reactivation in immunocompetent patients generally produces mild or no symptoms. Otherwise I fully agree with the final message regarding the importance of including tick-borne diseases in the FUO differential (empiric doxycycline in endemic areas is definitely a good idea). As a clinical note, normal platelets and WBC essentially rule out anaplasmosis. Great video!

comments.text:
Love hearing about complex cases and appreciated hearing how FUO is investigated in the outpatient setting. I have a couple of zebra diagnoses of my own and an extensive history of FUO that has largely never had any cause found even after extensive workup. I have a central line though so high or prolonged fever always leads to hospitalization. I didn’t even realize- which speaks to how much doctors don’t always take the time to fully explain things and their line of thinking- that the CT thing was typical or more broadly looking for infection because I have severe GI issues and always took CTs with fevers to mean we were worried about simply gastro related issues like obstruction or colitis. Though I recently came in with fever and pretty bad rigors (in the 90+ degree heatwave!) and abdominal CT ended up pointed us towards septic pneumonia. At least we had an answer (and a blood stream infection related to the central line that was leading to the lung involvement) but so many times in the past- and even prior to the more severe issues I have now- no answer. 

To further add to my zebra status- I’ve probably been diagnosed with mono a dozen times from my teens on yet each and every time my lab results come back showing I’ve somehow never even been exposed to the virus. And I assume that remains true now, and I’m nearing 40. Yet have this extensive history of fever and swollen lymph nodes. I’m going to be like 70 when mono finally comes for me, given my luck. 

Props for sorting this one out and avoiding the antibiotics until you saw a clear reason for them. And love that you got infectious disease involved even prior to having an answer. I’m not sure many other docs would’ve gone that route especially in the outpatient setting with a patient who had no other major symptoms but the fevers and that’s one more way this treatable infection may have gone undetected until there were worse complications doen the line. That and consulting the ER docs was awesome to see. This is what top notch primary care is and should be. That actual collaboration versus just writing referrals and washing one’s hands of the patient- something I’ve personally experienced too many times. And the specialists are often focused on just their specialty so no one is really seeing the full picture. That’s what every zebra/ complex or unusual presentation or illness deserves.

transcript: I had such a unique patient case to share with you. In fact, it's so unique that my residents and I are doing a full case write-up on it. I'm curious at which point you'll know what the diagnosis is. Leave a comment down below if you figure out before me. Let's get started. Be well. A 45-year-old gentleman presents for a one-day history of a 101 fever, that's Fahrenheit, and no other symptoms. He's evaluated by another member of my staff, is found to have feel well otherwise, have no other symptoms. The doctor that was seeing him diagnosed him with a likely a viral illness, unclear which one because it was so early in the course. We did a swab for COVID and flu, both which were negative.
